titolo: SVB – The $42 Billion Bank Run That Took One Day
descrizione:
On March 9, 2023, depositors tried to pull $42 billion out of Silicon Valley Bank in a single day. By the next morning, California regulators had closed the bank, and it became the second-largest bank failure in US history at the time. This documentary follows the investigation: how a fast-growing bank bought long-dated bonds with a deposit boom, what happened when interest rates rose, and how a few days of panic broke it.

All facts come from SEC filings, the Federal Reserve's April 2023 review by Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr, the FDIC and major newspapers. The video explains held-to-maturity accounting, uninsured deposits and the speed of digital bank runs, and what regulators and banks learned afterwards.

copertina.scena_rosso: A single red figure stands calmly at the top of the bank's steps, holding a bond portfolio folder while the building behind him cracks
copertina.scena_blu: Many blue figures rush toward the entrance with phones in hand, pulling money out through glowing screens
copertina.scena_oro: A large gold SVB vault door, half open and cracking, with gold coins pouring out and draining away

fatti: On Thursday, March 9, 2023, depositors tried to withdraw $42 billion from Silicon Valley Bank in a single day
That was about a quarter of the bank's deposits (about $173 billion at end of 2022)
The next day, Friday, March 10, 2023, California regulators closed the bank and appointed the FDIC as receiver
It became the second-largest bank failure in US history at the time, after Washington Mutual in 2008
Open question: how does a bank with $209 billion in assets fall in two days?
SVB, founded in 1983 in Santa Clara, California, served venture capital firms and tech startups
At end of 2022 it had about $209 billion in total assets, the 16th-largest US bank
Its deposits grew from about $62 billion at end of 2019 to about $189 billion at end of 2021
Growth was driven by the venture funding boom and low interest rates in 2020-2021
Most of its deposits were uninsured: above the $250,000 FDIC limit

capitoli.titolo: Too Much Money, Nowhere to Lend
fatti: Deposits grew faster than loans, so SVB invested heavily in securities
Its securities portfolio grew to about $128 billion at end of 2021, including mortgage-backed securities and Treasuries
Much of it was classified held-to-maturity (about $91 billion at end of 2022)
Long-dated bonds bought when rates were near zero lose market value when rates rise
Held-to-maturity accounting means those losses are not shown on the balance sheet unless the bonds are sold
The Federal Reserve began raising rates in March 2022 and raised them repeatedly through 2022
SVB's 10-K filed in 2023 showed about $15.1 billion in unrealized losses on held-to-maturity securities at end of 2022
That loss was nearly as large as the bank's roughly $16 billion in shareholders' equity
Startups burned cash and venture funding slowed, so deposits began to fall during 2022
The Fed's April 2023 review found SVB had not hedged its interest-rate risk, and had removed some hedges
On March 8, 2023, SVB announced it had sold about $21 billion of available-for-sale securities at a loss of about $1.8 billion
It also announced plans to raise about $2.25 billion in new capital
The announcement alarmed investors and venture capital firms
SVB's stock fell about 60% on March 9, 2023, wiping out billions in market value
Several venture firms reportedly advised portfolio companies to move their money
On March 9, 2023, customers tried to withdraw about $42 billion, with the transfers made mostly digitally
The bank had a negative cash balance of about $958 million at end of that day, according to California regulators
It expected a further withdrawal request of around $100 billion on March 10
On the morning of March 10, trading in its shares was halted and regulators closed the bank
The FDIC took control, in a failure widely seen as a first of its kind: a bank run driven by social media and mobile banking
On March 12, 2023, regulators also closed Signature Bank of New York
That day the Treasury, Federal Reserve and FDIC announced all SVB depositors, including uninsured ones, would have access to their money on Monday March 13
The Fed created the Bank Term Funding Program to lend against bonds at face value
The FDIC said the cost to its Deposit Insurance Fund from SVB's failure was estimated at about $20 billion
First Republic Bank failed on May 1, 2023 and was sold to JPMorgan Chase
The Fed's April 2023 review by Michael Barr found SVB's management failed to manage interest-rate and liquidity risk
It also found supervisors did not take sufficiently forceful action, and that the bank grew rapidly without matching oversight
SVB's holding company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on March 17, 2023
First Citizens BancShares agreed on March 26, 2023 to acquire SVB's deposits and loans
The 2018 law raising the threshold for stricter rules to $250 billion in assets was discussed as a factor, and SVB had about $209 billion
Answer to the opening question: the bank's assets were in long-dated bonds that had lost value, and its depositors were mostly uninsured and highly connected
A rumor-driven fear spread in hours because transfers were digital
Hidden losses in held-to-maturity bonds plus concentrated deposits turned a paper problem into a real run
Regulators and banks reviewed interest-rate risk, uninsured deposits and supervision after 2023
Ending line: Subscribe for the next one.
